value: Find an equation of the plane that contains the point $P(-3,2,1)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{n}= \langle 0, 2, 0 \rangle.$

First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=\langle -3,2,1 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{n}=\langle 0,2,0 \rangle$ is normal to the plane.

The equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{n}$ can be given as

$$
(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{p}) \cdot \mathbf{n} = 0,
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of any point on the plane, and $\mathbf p$ is the position vector of $P.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨0,2,0⟩ & =⟨-3,2,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,2,0⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨0,2,0⟩ & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

A nonzero vector $\langle 0,\, \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{b}, \: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{c} \rangle$ is parallel to the plane $\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle 2, -1, 4 \rangle  = 3.$ What is the value of $\dfrac{b}{c}?$

We need a vector $\mathbf{v} = \langle t_1,t_2,t_3 \rangle$ that is parallel to the given plane. 

From the equation $\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle 2, -1, 4 \rangle  = 3$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $\mathbf{n}=\langle 2, -1, 4 \rangle.$ So, $\mathbf{v} \perp \mathbf{n}$ and we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨2,-1,4⟩ & =0 \\ 2{t}_{1}-{t}_{2}+4{t}_{3} & =0 \\ {t}_{2} & =2{t}_{1}+4{t}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain 

$$
\mathbf{v}=\langle t_1, 2t_1 + 4t_3, t_3 \rangle,
$$

where $t_1,t_3 \in (-\infty,\infty).$ 

We are told that the first component of $\mathbf{v}$ equals $0.$ So, we must set $t_1=0.$ 

Since $\mathbf{v}$ is nonzero, we can pick any $t_3 \neq 0.$ For example, setting $t_3=1$, we get

$$
\mathbf{v} = \langle 0,\, \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{4}, \, \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{1} \rangle.
$$

Therefore, $\dfrac{b}{c} = 4.$

Find an equation of the plane that passes through the point $Q(\sqrt{2},0,-5)$ and is perpendicular to the line

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=3 \\ y &=-1+\sqrt{3}t \\ z &=5-t.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Note that the position vector of $Q$ is $\mathbf{q}=\langle \sqrt{2},0,-5 \rangle.$ Converting the parametric equations of the line to vector form, we get
$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}x = 3 \\ y = - 1 + \sqrt{3} t \\ z = 5 - t\end{array} \right. } \qquad  \Longrightarrow \qquad

\langle x, y, z \rangle= \langle 3, -1 , 5 \rangle
+t \ \underbrace{\langle 0 , \sqrt{3} , -1 \rangle}_{\large \mathbf{v}} .
$$

The direction vector of the line is $\mathbf{v}=\langle  0 , \sqrt{3} , -1\rangle,$ so a normal vector to the plane is 

$$
\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{v}=\langle  0 , \sqrt{3} , -1 \rangle.
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-q)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-q\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =q\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨0,\sqrt{3},-1⟩ & =⟨\sqrt{2},0,-5⟩\cdot ⟨0,\sqrt{3},-1⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨0,\sqrt{3},-1⟩ & =5.\end{aligned}
$$
Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(9,-2,3)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{n}=3\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j}+7\mathbf{k}.$

First, we note that the position vector of the point $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=\langle 9,-2,3 \rangle$ and the normal vector of the plane is $\mathbf{n}=\langle 3,-4,7 \rangle.$

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨3,-4,7⟩ & =⟨9,-2,3⟩\cdot ⟨3,-4,7⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨3,-4,7⟩ & =56.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $\mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨3,-4,7⟩ & =56 \\ 3x-4y+7z & =56 \\ 3x-4y+7z-56 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(-1,4,8)$ and is perpendicular to the line 
$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{x+3}{-5}=\dfrac{y-1}{3}=\dfrac{z+2}{2}.
$$

First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=\langle -1,4,8 \rangle.$ From the canonical equation, we find that the line is parallel to the vector $\langle -5,3,2 \rangle.$ So, the normal vector of the plane is 

$$
\mathbf{n}=\langle -5,3,2 \rangle.
$$

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-5,3,2⟩ & =⟨-1,4,8⟩\cdot ⟨-5,3,2⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-5,3,2⟩ & =33\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $\mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-5,3,2⟩ & =33 \\ -5x+3y+2z & =33 \\ -5x+3y+2z-33 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
Given the Cartesian equation $2x-y+z+13=0$ of the plane $\Pi,$ find an equation of $\Pi$ in the form $(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p})\cdot\mathbf{n}=0.$

First, from the coefficients in equation of the plane, we get that the normal vector of $\Pi$ is $\mathbf{n}=\langle 2,-1,1 \rangle.$

Now, we solve the Cartesian equation of $\Pi$ for $z\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-y+z+13 & =0 \\ z & =-2x+y-13\end{aligned}
$$

If we put, say, $x=0$ and $y=0,$ we get $z=-13.$ So, the point $P(0,0,-13)$ lies on $\Pi.$ Note that the position vector of $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=\langle 0,0,-13 \rangle.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ (r-⟨0,0,-13⟩)\cdot ⟨2,-1,1⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(-3,2,-6)$ and is parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{v_1}=\langle -3, 5, 2 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{v_2}=\langle 1, 3, -2 \rangle.$

First, we note that the position vector of the point $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=\langle -3,2,-6 \rangle.$

Now, we need to find the normal vector of the plane. To do that, we use the cross product of $\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\mathbf{v_2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & ={v}_{1}\times {v}_{2} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 5 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\times \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -3 & 5 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-16i-4j-14k \\  & =⟨-16,-4,-14⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-16,-4,-14⟩ & =⟨-3,2,-6⟩\cdot ⟨-16,-4,-14⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-16,-4,-14⟩ & =124\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $\mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-16,-4,-14⟩ & =124 \\ -16x-4y-14z & =124 \\ -16x-4y-14z-124 & =0 \\ 8x+2y+7z+62 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
Find a parametric equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(-3,2,5)$ and is parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{b}= \langle 17,3,15 \rangle$  and $\mathbf{c}= \langle 5,0,-8 \rangle.$

$$
\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{p}+ s\mathbf{b}+ t \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\mathbf{p}$ is the position vector of a point on the plane and the vectors $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ are parallel to the plane but not to each other.

Here, the position vector of the given point $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=\langle -3,2,5 \rangle,$ and the two vectors that are parallel to the plane (but not to each other) are $\mathbf{b}= \langle 17,3,15 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{c}= \langle 5,0,-8 \rangle.$

So, a parametric equation of the plane is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨-3,2,5⟩+s\,⟨17,3,15⟩+t\,⟨5,0,-8⟩,\,s,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Find a parametric equation of the plane that passes through the points $A(-1,4,-3),$ $B(7,5,4),$ and $C(2,-2,8).$

First, we need to find two vectors that are parallel to the plane (but not to each other). Let's use the displacement vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨7,5,4⟩-⟨-1,4,-3⟩ \\  & =⟨8,1,7⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =⟨2,-2,8⟩-⟨-1,4,-3⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-6,11⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we consider the position vector $\mathbf{a}=\langle -1,4,-3 \rangle$ of the point $A,$ then the corresponding parametric equation of the plane is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =a+s\overset{\to }{AB}+t\overset{\to }{AC} \\ r & =⟨-1,4,-3⟩+s⟨8,1,7⟩+t⟨3,-6,11⟩,\,s,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** The form of the final equation depends on our choice of vectors and the point on the plane. We could have picked other vectors. Likewise, we could have chosen $B$ or $C$ instead of $A$ as our point on the plane. So, the answer is *not unique*!

A nonzero vector $⟨a,\,b,\,0⟩$ is parallel to the plane $r\cdot ⟨6,-2,0⟩=-14.$ What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$

We need a vector $v=⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩$ that is parallel to the given plane.

$$

$$

Consider the subsets $\; A=\{ \langle x, y, z \rangle \in \mathbb{R}^3 : x^2=y \}\;$ and $\; B= \{ \langle 3-t, -3+t, -6+2t \rangle : t \in \mathbb{R} \}.\;$ Which of them is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3?$

Let's analyze each of the subsets.

- The set $A$ is not a subspace because it is not closed under scalar multiplication. For example, the vector $\mathbf{a}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}$ belongs to $A,$ but the vector $2\cdot \mathbf{a}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}$ does not lie in $A$ (because it does not satisfy $x^2=y$).

- The set $B$ represents a line, and a line is a subspace if and only if it passes through the origin. If the origin belongs to this subset, we would have
$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}3 - t \\ - 3 + t \\ - 6 + 2 t\end{array} \right]}=
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{array} \right]},
$$
which gives us

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3-t &=0 \\ -3+t &=0 \\ -6+2t &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We see that $t=3$ is the solution to the three equations. So, if we choose $t=3,$ then we find that $\mathbf{0} \in B.$ Therefore, $B$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3.$

In conclusion, the correct answer is "$B$ only".

$$

$$

 

Now, we need to find the normal vector of the plane. To do that, we use the cross product of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & ={v}_{1}\times {v}_{2} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\times \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-5i+j+2k \\  & =⟨-5,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-5,1,2⟩ & =⟨2,0,3⟩\cdot ⟨-5,1,2⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-5,1,2⟩ & =-4\end{aligned}

$$

Which of the following sets is a subspace of ${R}^{3}?$

Select all that apply.

Let's analyze each of the subsets.

- The set $A$ is not a subspace because it does not contain the zero vector. Indeed, $0=⟨0,0,0⟩$ does not satisfy the equation $1-x-y=0$ since $1-0-0\ne 0.$

- The set $B$ is not a subspace. Indeed, the vector $u=⟨1,0,0⟩$ is in $B$, but $2u=⟨2,0,0⟩$ is not in $B$, since ${2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}≰1.$ So, $B$ is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- The set $C$ is a subspace. It represents a plane, and a plane is a subspace if and only if it passes through the origin. Here, the components of the zero vector $0=⟨0,0,0⟩$ satisfy the equation $2x+3y-z=0$ since $2\cdot 0+3\cdot 0-0=0.$ So $0$ lies in $C.$

\displaystyle \begin{gathered}C=\left\{\begin{gathered}⟨x,y,z⟩\in {R}^{3}:\\2x+3y-z=0\end{gathered}\right\}\end{gathered}
$$ only.

lies outside the subset.

$$

$$

which we can write as

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
16{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}<144.
$$

$$

Which of the following sets is a subspace of ${R}^{3}?$

I. $A=\{t\cdot ⟨2,-4,1⟩\,:\,t\in R\}$

II. $B=\{⟨x,y,z⟩\in {R}^{3}:xzy=1\}$

III. $C=\{⟨x,y,z⟩\in {R}^{3}:{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}>0\}$

Let's analyze each of the subsets.

- The set $A$ is a subspace. It represents a line, and a line is a subspace if and only if it passes through the zero vector, $0.$ This can be verified by taking $t=0$, since 

$$
0\cdot ⟨2,-4,1⟩=⟨0,0,0⟩.
$$

So, $0$ lies in $A.$

- The set $B$ is not a subspace because it does not contain the zero vector. Indeed, $0=⟨0,0,0⟩$ does not satisfy the equation $xyz=1$ since $0\cdot 0\cdot 0\ne 1.$

- The set $C$ is not a subspace because it does not contain the zero vector. Indeed, $0=⟨0,0,0⟩$ does not satisfy the inequality ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}>0$ since ${0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}=0.$

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I only."

III. $C=\{⟨x,y⟩\in {R}^{2}:x=y=0\}$

Let's analyze each of the subsets.

- The set $A$ is a line, but it is not a subspace because it does not contain the zero vector. Indeed, $0=⟨0,0⟩$ does not satisfy the equation $x+y=1$ since $0+0\ne 1.$

- The set $B$ is a subspace. It represents a line, and a line is a subspace if and only if it passes through the origin. Here, the components of the zero vector $0=⟨0,0⟩$ satisfy the equation $x=0$ since $0=0.$ So, $0$ lies in $B.$

- The set $C$ consists only of the vector $⟨0,0⟩$, which is a special (trivial) subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

So, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Suppose we know that a plane $\Pi$ passes through the point $P(1,1,2)$ and that the vector $\mathbf{n}=\langle 0,0,3 \rangle$ is perpendicular to the plane. Let's write down an equation of this plane using the dot product.

![](images/0f/0f8353480099369ad92701d1799f72d46eab4bbe5c17add8cb37a4f34074311b.png)

We start by considering an arbitrary point $R(x,y,z)$ that lies on the plane. The position vectors of the points $R$ and $P$ are $\mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle$ and $\mathbf{p}=\langle 1,1,2 \rangle$ respectively. So, the vector

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PR} & =r-p \\  & =r-⟨1,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

is parallel to the plane. Therefore, $\overrightarrow{PR} \perp \mathbf{n},$ as shown below.

![](images/28/28b6770bd681257b1030679a421b80e3f3d1e8fbb86d2060b64c7301d0878c5c.png)

Now, recall that if two nonzero vectors are perpendicular, then their dot product is zero:

$$
\overrightarrow{PR}\perp \mathbf{n} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \overrightarrow{PR}\cdot \mathbf{n} = 0
$$

So, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is called the **vector equation of the plane** that passes through the point $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{n}.$ In our case, we obtain

$$
(\mathbf{r} - \langle 1,1,2 \rangle) \cdot \langle 0,0,3 \rangle = 0.
$$

**Note:** Using the properties of the dot product, we can arrive at an alternative vector equation given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot n & =c\end{aligned}
$$

where $c = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n}$ is a (scalar) constant.

If we are given an equation of a plane using the dot product, we can always obtain an equation in terms of $x,$ $y,$ and $z.$ For example, suppose we have the plane that passes through the point $P(-7,5,-2)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{n}=\langle 3,-6,5 \rangle.$

First, we note that the position vector of the point $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=\langle -7,5,-2 \rangle,$ and we can write down the equation of the plane using the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ & =⟨-7,5,-2⟩\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ & =-61\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation, we substitute $\mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ & =-61 \\ 3x-6y+5z & =-61 \\ 3x-6y+5z+61 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This final equation is called the **Cartesian equation of the plane**.

![](images/77/77f18981dda500889655225eabbec730b7b295e6b16cec1700d56c2e27e0ac91.png)

Note that in the equation 

$$
{\color{blue}3}x+({\color{blue}-6})y+{\color{blue}5}z+61 = 0,
$$

the coefficients next to $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ are the coordinates of the normal vector 

$$
\mathbf{n}=\langle {\color{blue}3},{\color{blue}-6},{\color{blue}5} \rangle
$$

.

Any plane can be uniquely determined by a point and two non-parallel direction vectors. For example, let $\Pi$ be the plane that passes through the point $P(1,0,2)$ and is parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{b}= \langle 0,3,0 \rangle$  and $\mathbf{c}= \langle -1,1,1 \rangle.$

![](images/ea/ea4ce822abec2b68d2471a2787f4e045493ca43c1c6795a7e0069de80cb5adee.png)

Using the vectors $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c},$ we can construct a **parametric equation** of the plane.

First, let $R$ be any general point in the plane, with position vector $\mathbf{r}.$ Notice that we can get from $P$ to $R$ using a linear combination of $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ with some (unknown for us) coefficients $s$ and $t$, as shown below.

![](images/b4/b40f91c3d75f092c7b29f19770364e7518d37b64ba594a311a762ad79a950e4f.png)

So, we can write the **parametric equation** of the plane as

$$
{\color{red}\mathbf{r}} = \mathbf{p}+s{\color{blue}\,\mathbf{b}}+t\,{\color{blue}\mathbf{c}},
	\qquad s,t \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

This formula works whenever $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ are not parallel.

In our case, $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ are indeed not parallel to each other. So, using column vector notation, the parametric equation for the plane $\Pi$ is given by
$$
\mathbf{r} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{array} \right]} + s {\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{array} \right]} + t {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]},
	\qquad s,t \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

Any plane can be uniquely determined by three non-collinear points. 

![](images/08/08e65c4e3465a4bf155dfed6bc0dc2a35bf2eb9326d9bff0c0aa75b86e97d76b.png)

To write down a parametric equation of the plane, the trick is to use the three non-collinear points to construct two displacement vectors that are parallel to the plane.

![](images/16/1613ea9df76b637b93e0e4b38b70b87892140398eaa7aaccb74f2a5642124dfd.png)

Then we can proceed as usual to find the equation of the plane. Let's practice this technique in the following example.

Suppose we have a plane with the following normal vector: 

$$
\mathbf{n}=\langle -1,2,1 \rangle
$$

Let's use the scalar product to find a vector that is parallel to this plane.

We denote our parallel vector as $\mathbf{v} = \langle t_1,t_2,t_3 \rangle.$ Now, since $\mathbf{v} \perp \mathbf{n},$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,2,1⟩ & =0 \\ -{t}_{1}+2{t}_{2}+{t}_{3} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to find a nonzero solution to this equation. To do that, we solve the equation for *one* of the variables (it doesn't matter which one). For example, let's solve our equation for the variable $t_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =2{t}_{2}+{t}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the variable $t_1$ depends on $t_2$ and $t_3,$ which, in turn, can be *any* real numbers. The variables $t_2$ and $t_3$ are called **free variables**.

Hence, the general form of our vector $\mathbf{v}$ is

$$
\mathbf{v}=\langle 2t_2+t_3, \, t_2, \, t_3 \rangle,
$$

where $t_2, t_3 \in (-\infty,\infty).$

To find a particular vector parallel to the plane, we can substitute any values for $t_2$ and $t_3\mathbin{:}$

- For example, setting $t_2=0$ and $t_3=1$, we get

$$
\mathbf{v}_1= \langle 1, 0, 1 \rangle.
$$

- Or, we could set $t_2=1$ and $t_3=0$ and get

$$
\mathbf{v}_2 = \langle 2, 1, 0 \rangle.
$$

**Note:** There are infinitely many vectors parallel to a given plane. In our example, we found only two particular vectors.

Recall that $H\subseteq \mathbb R^n$ is a **subspace** of $\mathbb{R}^n$ if and only if it satisfies the following properties:

- *Closure under vector addition:* 

$\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are in $H,$ then their sum $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ is also in $H.$

- *Closure under scalar multiplication:* 

$\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ is in $H,$ then $c\cdot \mathbf{u}$ is also in $H$ for any scalar number $c.$

In the vector space $\mathbb{R}^n,$ there are two **trivial subspaces**.

- One trivial subspace is the set 

$$
H=\{\mathbf{0}\}
$$

 consisting of just the zero vector. This is a subspace because the sum of two zero vectors is the zero vector, and any multiple of the zero vector is the zero vector.

- Another trivial subspace is the set 

$$
H = \mathbb{R}^n
$$

Recall that the cross product of two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ is defined as

$$
\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b} = | \, \mathbf{a} \, | \cdot | \, \mathbf{b} \, | \cdot \sin\theta \cdot \mathbf{n},
$$

where

- $\theta$ is the angle formed between the vectors when their tails are placed at the same point, and

- $\mathbf{n}$ is a unit vector that's perpendicular to *both* $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}.$

The cross product satisfies a few properties that we would normally expect multiplication to satisfy. 

Specifically, given the vectors $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ $\mathbf{c},$ and any scalar $\lambda,$ the following properties hold.

- The cross product distributes over addition and subtraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}(a\pm b)\times c & =a\times c\pm b\times c \\ c\times (a\pm b) & =c\times a\pm c\times b\end{aligned}
$$

- The cross product is associative with respect to scalar multiplication:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda a)\times b & =\lambda (a\times b) \\ a\times (\lambda b) & =\lambda (a\times b)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see some examples of how we can use these properties.

The cross product depends on the order of multiplication! In other words, the cross product is *not* commutative. 

More specifically, it is **anticommutative**, meaning that if we swap the order of the multiplication, the result changes sign:

$$
\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = -\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a}
$$

To understand why this is so, we need to go back to the right-hand rule for calculating $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b{:}$

![](images/05/058021724be36344bb806683afaa0a4243e63a3c540927388346ddb447422b4e.png)

 Recall that the right-hand rule says that we calculate the *direction* of the vector $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b$ as follows:

- First, we extend the index finger on our right hand along the direction of $\mathbf{a}.$

- Then, we extend our middle finger along the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

- When we do this, our thumb points in the direction of $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/42/4295a74c02deebee63d9db0f369d7f8b8d8a3956d9dcb59bd58fec19f450e07d.png)

We can also use the right-hand rule to calculate the direction of $\mathbf b \times \mathbf a{:}$

- First, we extend the index finger on our right hand along the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

- Then, we extend our middle finger along the direction of $\mathbf{a}.$

- When we do this, our thumb points in the direction of $\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}.$

![](images/81/818db143964d23937a18fc44e7546e5a932b87f79a5b19737833d10ed08215d9.png)

So, $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b$ and $\mathbf b \times \mathbf a$ have the *same* magnitude yet *opposite* direction. Therefore,

$$
\mathbf a \times \mathbf b = -\mathbf b \times \mathbf a.
$$
